strengths: Clear, well-motivated technical contribution: decomposing interaction into pre-interaction/interaction/post-interaction phases and associating each with the 'dominant' object's features is an intuitive and effective solution to the multi-object feature entanglement problem in prior trajectory-controlled video generation methods (Tora, DragAnything).

Comprehensive baseline comparison: all key baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, IRASim) are retrained on the same curated dataset for fair comparison, and RoboMaster consistently outperforms them across FVD, PSNR, SSIM, trajectory error, and most VBench metrics.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, collaborative vs. separate trajectories, motion injector vs. cross-attention), and additional robustness analyses (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation) support the practical claims about tolerance to imprecise user input.

Strong qualitative and generalization evidence: extensive in-the-wild results (diverse OOD objects, diverse manipulation skills, auto-regressive long video generation) suggest the method generalizes beyond the training distribution (Bridge V2).

Good attention to usability: the annotation scheme (brush mask + phase-segmented trajectory) is simpler for users than requiring complete dual trajectories, and a user study (with 47% preference vs ~20% for the next best) supports perceptual quality gains.
Detailed reproducibility information provided in supplementary (dataset curation pipeline, network architecture table, Gradio annotation tool description).
weaknesses: No downstream validation of the stated motivating use case (generating robotic decision-making/training data) -- e.g., no experiments showing that policies trained on RoboMaster-generated videos improve over policies trained with baseline-generated videos or real data alone. This is the primary claimed application in the introduction but is left unvalidated.

VBench metric improvements (Table 3) are often marginal (e.g., aesthetic/imaging quality differ by <1 point and RoboMaster sometimes underperforms Tora on Aesthetic Quality), raising questions about the practical significance of the gains beyond FVD/trajectory error.

Evaluation relies on a single dataset (Bridge V2) with a fairly small test set (214 samples) for the main quantitative comparisons; broader multi-embodiment or multi-dataset validation would strengthen claims of general applicability.

The dominant/submissive object formulation appears limited to two-entity interactions; it is unclear how the framework would scale to manipulations involving three or more interacting objects, which is not discussed or tested.
No failure case analysis or discussion of when/why the collaborative trajectory design might break down beyond the brief generic limitations paragraph.

Statistical significance/variance is not reported for any of the quantitative comparisons (single-run point estimates), making it hard to judge robustness of the reported gains, especially the small VBench deltas.

Method is built entirely on top of a large pretrained CogVideoX-5B backbone; compute cost, training/inference efficiency, and comparison of parameter overhead of the motion injector relative to baselines is not discussed, limiting insight into practical deployment cost.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and relevant limitation of prior trajectory-controlled video generation methods (Tora, DragAnything, etc.): feature entanglement when robot and object trajectories overlap during interaction, illustrated clearly in Fig 2.

The phase-decomposition idea (pre-interaction/interaction/post-interaction, with dominant-subject feature switching) is intuitive and reasonably well-motivated by the physical dynamics of manipulation.
Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: retrains all baselines on the same curated Bridge V2 data, reports FVD/PSNR/SSIM/TrajError plus VBench sub-metrics, and includes a user study.

Multiple ablations (causal embedding, point vs. mask representation, separate vs collaborative trajectories, cross-attention injection, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation) that at least partially support the design choices.

Demonstrates qualitative generalization to in-the-wild/OOD objects and supports an interactive annotation tool (Gradio demo) and auto-regressive long-video generation, which adds some practical value.
weaknesses: No downstream validation of the paper's central claimed application: despite motivating the work as producing 'robotic decision-making data' for policy learning, there is no experiment showing that generated videos actually improve a downstream manipulation policy (e.g., imitation learning, inverse dynamics, or planning success rate). This is a critical missing piece given the stated motivation in the introduction.

The quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (Tora) are modest and inconsistent: FVD improves only ~3% (147.31 vs 152.28), PSNR/SSIM differences are marginal, and on VBench (Table 3) RoboMaster is not even best on Aesthetic Quality (50.32 vs Tora's 50.61); only TrajError shows a clearer margin.

The comparison between mask-based (ours) and point-based (Tora/MotionCtrl) representations is not architecturally fair: masks inherently encode shape/extent information that points do not, so part of the improvement may simply stem from richer conditioning input rather than the proposed collaborative-trajectory formulation itself. An ablation isolating the contribution of mask vs. collaborative decomposition independent of representation richness is missing.

Ablations do not isolate the core subject-embedding module (appearance+shape circular volume) against a no-embedding baseline; only a 'causal embedding' ablation is reported, leaving the standalone benefit of Sec 3.2's design under-verified.

Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (Bridge V2) with 214 test samples; no cross-dataset or cross-embodiment evaluation is provided despite the paper itself noting generalization to varied embodiments as a limitation—raising concerns about the generality of the reported SOTA claims.

The annotation pipeline for training data relies on a hand-tuned motion threshold τ to detect interaction phase boundaries (Appendix A.1), with no sensitivity analysis or quantification of annotation/filtering error rates, which undermines reproducibility and reliability claims.

The claimed simplification in user interaction is questionable: users must still specify phase boundary frames and a full collaborative trajectory with object masks, which is arguably comparable or more complex than prior point/mask annotation schemes, despite the paper framing it as simpler.
The user study methodology (number of participants, instructions, blind comparison protocol) is not described, limiting the reliability of the reported 47.33% preference metric.
There are reference-list inconsistencies (e.g., entries [17] and [18] are duplicate citations of the same 'Motion Prompting' paper), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

Technical novelty is incremental: the core contribution amounts to reorganizing existing trajectory/mask conditioning mechanisms into a 3-phase schedule within an existing CogVideoX-5B backbone, with relatively small architecture modifications (a lightweight motion injector), which may be viewed as engineering refinement rather than a substantial methodological advance.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies concrete feature entanglement issues in multi-object interaction regions for trajectory-controlled robotic video generation, and motivates the solution well with a clear qualitative example (Fig 2).

Novel collaborative trajectory decomposition (pre-interaction, interaction, post-interaction) driven by dominant/submissive object modeling is an intuitive and technically sound idea that differs meaningfully from prior isolated-trajectory approaches (Tora, DragAnything, MotionCtrl).

Comprehensive comparison against four strong, fairly-retrained baselines on the same dataset/backbone (CogVideoX-5B), with multiple metric families (FVD, PSNR, SSIM, TrajError, VBench) plus a user study showing a large preference gap (47% vs runner-up 21%).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of causal embedding, mask vs point-based subject representation, collaborative vs separate trajectories, and injection mechanism (cross-attention vs the proposed conv-based injector), which support the design choices.

Practical usability contributions: brush-based mask input, decomposed sub-trajectory annotation (rather than full dual trajectories), and demonstrated robustness to sparse/coarse masks and trajectory perturbations (Tables 5-6), which strengthens the system's real-world applicability.

Strong qualitative generalization to diverse in-the-wild objects/scenes and skills (Fig 5, 6, S10, S11), and an auto-regressive long-video generation extension, indicating good transfer beyond the training distribution despite training only on Bridge V2.
Reasonably detailed supplementary material including dataset curation pipeline, network architecture table, and annotation tool description, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains over baselines on many metrics are fairly modest (e.g., PSNR 21.55 vs Tora's 21.24, SSIM 0.803 vs 0.788), and on VBench the method does not uniformly win across all sub-metrics (e.g., Aesthetic Quality is lower than Tora), which undercuts the claim of 'consistently outperforming' prior work.

No downstream validation that the generated videos actually improve robot policy learning (e.g., via imitation learning or as augmented training data), despite the paper's stated motivation of producing 'high-quality robotic data' for scalable robot learning — this leaves the central practical claim unverified.

Evaluation is conducted on a single dataset (Bridge V2) with a modest test set (214 samples); no comparison against more recent 3D/depth-aware trajectory control methods mentioned in related work (e.g., 3DTrajMaster, LeviTor, ObjCtrl-2.5D), despite these being discussed as relevant prior art.

The automatic phase-segmentation procedure (motion threshold τ to detect interaction start/end) is only briefly described and its robustness/sensitivity is not analyzed; errors here could propagate into training data quality, but no failure-rate or filtering statistics are reported.
No report of variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance for the reported metrics, and no analysis of inference-time/computational overhead relative to baselines.

The three-phase decomposition assumes a relatively clean separation between pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction; for more continuous or ambiguous manipulation types (e.g., wiping, pouring) it is unclear how phase boundaries are defined or how sensitive results are to this assumption.

The method's dependence on accurate object/mask detection (Grounded-SAM) or user-provided masks introduces a potential failure mode that is only partially addressed via the mask-sparsity ablation, without deeper analysis of catastrophic segmentation failures.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: clearly identifies feature entanglement in overlapping regions as a key limitation of prior object-decomposed trajectory methods (Tora, DragAnything), and proposes an intuitive fix via phase-decomposed (pre/interaction/post) collaborative trajectories.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple axes: visual quality (FVD/PSNR/SSIM/VBench), trajectory accuracy, a substantial user study (45% preference vs 17.74% for best baseline), and downstream robotic policy success rates on RLBench and SIMPLER.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of causal embedding, mask- vs point-based object representation, collaborative vs separate trajectories, and injection mechanism (cross-attention vs conv-based), along with robustness analyses to mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts.

Practical contributions beyond the core method: a new 21k video-trajectory annotated dataset from Bridge, a user-friendly Gradio annotation tool, and clear discussion of how the design simplifies user interaction (brush masks, partial trajectory specification).

Honest and detailed limitations section (3D generalization, automatic segmentation failure rates on multi-object scenes, novel robot morphology generalization) with supporting quantitative evidence (e.g., Grounded-SAM success rates), which strengthens the paper's credibility.

Demonstrates generalization to diverse in-the-wild/out-of-domain objects and long, multi-step autoregressive video generation, indicating the method is not narrowly overfit to Bridge-specific scenarios.
weaknesses: Downstream action-planning results (Table 4) are mixed rather than uniformly superior: RoboMaster underperforms Tora on several tasks (e.g., put knife 0.76 vs 0.82, open microwave 0.54 vs 0.61), which somewhat undercuts the claim of consistently 'more reliable interaction videos' translating into better policies.

The improvement margins on standard video-quality metrics (PSNR 21.55 vs 21.24, SSIM 0.803 vs 0.788 relative to Tora) are fairly small despite a large gap in user preference, raising questions about whether FVD/PSNR/SSIM adequately capture the qualitative gains being claimed, and inviting concern about cherry-picked qualitative examples in Fig. 5/6.

Practical annotation burden is non-trivial: the method still depends on accurate phase transition detection/annotation (F1, F2), and automatic tools (Grounded-SAM) achieve only 0.14–0.21 success on multi-object scenes, meaning substantial manual curation was needed for the training set and would likely be needed at deployment/scale.

Core novelty is somewhat incremental — reframing trajectory decomposition from an object axis to a temporal/phase axis, combined with fairly standard mask-based appearance/shape embeddings and a lightweight conv-based injector — rather than introducing fundamentally new modeling machinery.

Main quantitative comparisons and dataset curation rely solely on Bridge for training the primary model; RLBench/SIMPLER are used only for a small-scale post-training/adaptation stage (1,300 pairs), limiting the strength of claims about broad applicability across embodiments and environments.

Some methodological details remain underspecified for reproducibility, e.g., precise criteria/thresholds for automatic phase segmentation (motion threshold τ), and how failure cases in transition detection are handled during training versus filtered out.

strengths: Identifies a real and well-motivated problem: feature entanglement in overlapping regions when prior trajectory-controlled video generation methods (Tora, DragAnything) model robot arm and manipulated object with separate/decentralized trajectories.

The phase decomposition (pre-interaction / interaction / post-interaction) combined with dominant/submissive object assignment is a reasonably intuitive and relatively novel way to unify multi-object trajectory conditioning.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple axes: video quality (FVD/PSNR/SSIM), trajectory accuracy, VBench metrics, user study, and downstream robotic action-planning success rates on RLBench and SIMPLER, which goes beyond pure video-metric evaluation and ties generation quality to policy performance.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (causal embedding, point vs. mask representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, cross-attention injection, mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, prompt corruption) that support individual design choices.
Practical contributions for usability: brush-based mask annotation, simplified sub-trajectory annotation, and a Gradio demo pipeline, plus a curated 21k video-trajectory dataset from Bridge.
Candid and fairly detailed limitations/appendix discussion, including honest reporting of Grounded-SAM failure rates and unresolved challenges in 3D control and novel robot morphology generalization.
weaknesses: Quantitative improvements over the strongest baseline (Tora) in Table 2 are fairly modest in absolute terms (FVD 152.28→147.31, PSNR 21.24→21.55, SSIM 0.788→0.803), raising questions about whether the architectural novelty translates into a clearly significant gain beyond the large jump in the (less standardized, less detailed) user-preference study.

Action planning results in Table 4 are mixed — RoboMaster underperforms Tora on 'put knife' and 'open microwave', undercutting the claim that more accurate interaction modeling consistently yields better downstream policies.

The core technical contributions (phase-decomposed trajectory conditioning, mask-based circular volume embeddings, zero-init conv motion injector) are largely engineering refinements layered on an existing pretrained backbone (CogVideoX-5B) rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm.

Heavy reliance on manual annotation/correction in dataset curation (Grounded-SAM success rates as low as 0.14 for multi-object scenes) undermines the scalability narrative central to the paper's motivation (addressing data scarcity).

The dominant/submissive, three-phase decomposition is a simplifying assumption that may not generalize cleanly to tasks with simultaneous multi-object interactions, bimanual manipulation, or continuous/non-discrete interaction phases — a limitation not deeply explored empirically beyond a few OOD qualitative examples.
User study methodology (number of raters, blinding, statistical significance) is not described, weakening confidence in the large reported preference margin (45.16% vs 17.74%).

Reported ablations for robustness (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, prompt corruption) use relative PSNR percentages rather than absolute quality metrics, making it harder to judge real-world significance of the reported robustness.
Generalization to novel robot embodiments remains unsolved and is acknowledged as an open problem, limiting the practical impact of the proposed system for broader robot learning deployment.

Baselines are retrained versions of prior methods under the authors' own curated data/pipeline, and no comparison is made against newer/stronger open video generation backbones, leaving open the possibility that comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples with the current state of the art.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifies a specific limitation (feature entanglement in overlapping regions) in prior trajectory-conditioned video generation methods for robotic manipulation, illustrated concretely in Fig. 2.

The collaborative trajectory formulation, decomposing interaction into pre-interaction/interaction/post-interaction phases and associating dominant/submissive object features with each, is a reasonable and intuitive design that is clearly explained and ablated.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple axes: visual quality (FVD/PSNR/SSIM), trajectory accuracy, user study, VBench metrics, and downstream robotic action planning on RLBench and SIMPLER with an inverse-dynamics pipeline.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies (causal embedding, point vs. mask representation, separate vs. collaborative trajectories, cross-attention injection, robustness to mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Practical usability contributions: mask-based brush annotation and simplified trajectory specification lower the burden on users compared to prior full-trajectory annotation schemes, and a Gradio demo/dataset pipeline is documented in detail.

Strong qualitative and quantitative demonstration of generalization to out-of-domain objects and diverse manipulation skills, along with candid, detailed limitation discussions (3D control, automatic segmentation reliability, novel robot morphologies) in the appendix.
Contribution of a curated 21k video-trajectory dataset from Bridge with a documented (semi-)automatic annotation pipeline.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contributions (phase decomposition of trajectories, mask-based circular-volume embeddings, zero-init conv injection) are relatively straightforward extensions of existing trajectory-conditioning and object-embedding techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Gains over the strongest baseline (Tora) are sometimes modest or inconsistent — e.g., in Table 4, RoboMaster underperforms Tora on 'put knife' and 'open microwave', and TesserAct/Tora are competitive on several tasks, tempering the 'new SOTA' framing in the abstract.

The action-planning evaluation is based on only 100 trials per task without reported variance/error bars, and the pipeline (video→inverse dynamics→action) introduces multiple potential confounds not fully disentangled from the video generation quality itself.

Reliance on automatic annotation (Grounded-SAM) for dataset construction is reported to have very low success rates in multi-object scenes (0.14–0.21), requiring substantial manual re-annotation; this practical bottleneck limits the scalability claims of the approach despite being framed as a strength.

Robustness/ablation tables (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, imperfect prompts) report only relative PSNR degradation without comparison to how baselines behave under the same perturbations, making it hard to assess whether the claimed robustness is a genuine advantage over prior methods.

The method still requires object-level dominant/submissive role parsing from the prompt, which may be brittle for prompts with ambiguous or multiple candidate objects; this failure mode is only partially addressed via the appendix's OOD discussion.

No analysis of computational overhead/inference latency relative to baselines, which is relevant given the added trajectory/mask-embedding components in an already large diffusion backbone (CogVideoX-5B).
